o: It lies on the side wall of the pelvis lateral to the rectum

The inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus lies on the side wall of the pelvis lateral to the rectum, within the parietal pelvic fascia.
It is at risk in rectal surgery, causing bladder and sexual dysfunction. (Last's p. 399)
Its parasympathetic fibres come from S2, 3 and 4

Its parasympathetic fibres come from S2, S3 and S4 through the pelvic splanchnic nerves.
Sympathetic fibres arrive via the hypogastric nerves. (Last's p. 399)
It measures about 2 cm anteroposteriorly

Last's says the plexus measures nearly 5 cm anteroposteriorly (and 2 cm vertically), not 2 cm anteroposteriorly.
A dimension trap. (Last's p. 399)
All parasympathetic fibres relay in its ganglia

The parasympathetic fibres pass through the plexus and relay in the walls of the viscera. Only some sympathetic fibres relay in its ganglia.
Parasympathetic ganglia lie close to or in their targets. (Last's p. 399)

questions.s: Motor supply of the pelvic viscera (Last's):
o: The detrusor is supplied by the pelvic splanchnics

The parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) are the motor supply to the detrusor, so they empty the bladder.
Damage causes urinary retention. (Last's p. 399)
The internal urethral sphincter is supplied through the superior hypogastric plexus

The internal urethral sphincter is supplied by sympathetic fibres coming through the superior hypogastric plexus.
It closes during ejaculation. (Last's p. 399)
The internal anal sphincter is supplied by the pelvic splanchnics

The internal anal sphincter is supplied by sympathetic fibres (from sacral sympathetic ganglia) through the pelvic plexus, not by the pelvic splanchnics.
The pelvic splanchnics relax it. (Last's p. 399)
Pain from the uterine body runs with the pelvic splanchnics

Pain from the body of the uterus runs with the hypogastric (sympathetic) nerves to T10 to L1. Pain from the lower cervix runs with the parasympathetics.
The pain pathway follows the "pelvic pain line". (Last's p. 399)

questions.s: Parasympathetic and sympathetic roles in the pelvis (Last's):
o: The pelvic splanchnics supply the colon from the splenic flexure distally

Pelvic splanchnic fibres run up through the hypogastric plexuses or behind the peritoneum to supply the hindgut, from the splenic flexure down to the rectum.
The vagus supplies proximal to this. (Last's p. 399-400)
Sympathetics are motor to the ductus deferens and seminal vesicles

Sympathetic fibres contract the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and prostatic muscle (emission), and the bladder neck sphincter.
Erection is parasympathetic. (Last's p. 399-400)
The descending colon receives sensory supply from pelvic splanchnics

The sensory supply of the descending colon is sympathetic; pain from it travels with sympathetic fibres.
The pelvic splanchnics carry sensation from the rectum and lower pelvic organs. (Last's p. 399-400)
Rectal pain is referred to L1 dermatome

Rectal pain carried by the pelvic splanchnics is referred to S2 to S4 (posterior femoral cutaneous territory), mimicking sciatica, not to L1.
Visceral pain refers to the dermatomes of its afferent segments. (Last's p. 399-400)
Stretch afferents travel in the pelvic splanchnic nerves

Stretch afferents from the bladder travel in the pelvic splanchnic nerves to the sacral segments.
They trigger the micturition reflex. (Last's p. 382-3)
The detrusor motor centre lies in the medial pontine reticular formation

Last's says a detrusor motor centre lies in the medial pontine reticular formation, controlled by a cortical inhibitory centre; reticulospinal fibres descend to the sacral cord.
This pontine micturition centre coordinates detrusor and sphincter. (Last's p. 382-3)
The external sphincter is supplied by the inferior rectal nerve

The external urethral sphincter is supplied by the perineal branch of the pudendal nerve. The inferior rectal nerve supplies the external anal sphincter.
Different branches of the pudendal nerve. (Last's p. 382-3)
Destruction of the sacral segments causes automatic reflex emptying

Destruction of the sacral segments paralyses the detrusor, causing overflow incontinence. Automatic reflex emptying follows transection above S2.
Upper motor neurone bladder empties reflexly; lower motor neurone bladder overflows. (Last's p. 382-3)
Its apex attaches to the transverse process of L5

The iliolumbar ligament is a sideways V whose apex is on the L5 transverse process, with upper and lower bands fanning out to the ilium.
It anchors L5 to the pelvis. (Last's p. 414)
Its upper band gives partial origin to quadratus lumborum

Its upper band runs to the iliac crest, gives partial origin to quadratus lumborum and is continuous with the lumbar fascia.
So it forms part of the posterior abdominal wall. (Last's p. 414)
Its lower band blends with the dorsal sacroiliac ligament

The lower band blends with the ventral sacroiliac ligament, not the dorsal one.
It lies in front of the joint. (Last's p. 414)
Its upper band attaches to the ischial spine

The upper band attaches to the iliac crest, not the ischial spine.
The sacrospinous ligament attaches to the ischial spine. (Last's p. 414)
It arises from S2, 3 and 4

The pudendal nerve arises from the anterior divisions of S2, S3 and S4.
It supplies the perineum. (Last's p. 414)
It lies medial to the pudendal vessels

The pudendal nerve leaves the pelvis below piriformis and crosses the sacrospinous ligament medial to the internal pudendal vessels before entering the pudendal canal.
So the nerve is the most medial structure at this point. (Last's p. 414)
The inferior rectal nerve supplies the internal anal sphincter

The inferior rectal nerve supplies the external anal sphincter (striated), not the internal sphincter (smooth muscle).
The internal sphincter has autonomic supply. (Last's p. 414)
The dorsal nerve of the penis supplies the skin of the dorsum at the root

The skin of the dorsum of the penis at its root is supplied by the ilioinguinal nerve (L1), not the dorsal nerve.
The dorsal nerve supplies the rest of the penis. (Last's p. 414)
It arises by eight digitations from the lower eight ribs

External oblique arises by eight digitations from the lower eight ribs. Its upper four slips interdigitate with serratus anterior and its lower four with latissimus dorsi.
The fibres run down and forward ("hands in pockets"). (Last's p. 414)
Its lower aponeurotic border forms the inguinal ligament

Between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle the free lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis is rolled in as the inguinal ligament.
It forms the floor of the inguinal canal. (Last's p. 414)
Its upper four digitations interdigitate with latissimus dorsi

The upper four digitations interdigitate with serratus anterior; the lower four with latissimus dorsi.
The statement swaps them. (Last's p. 414)
Its posterior muscular border forms the posterior boundary of the lumbar triangle

The posterior muscular border of external oblique forms the anterior boundary of the lumbar triangle (of Petit). Latissimus dorsi forms the posterior boundary.
The iliac crest forms the base. (Last's p. 414)
The internal oblique arises from the lateral two-thirds of the inguinal ligament

Internal oblique arises from the lumbar fascia, the anterior two-thirds of the iliac crest and the lateral two-thirds of the inguinal ligament.
Transversus arises from only the lateral half of the ligament. (Last's p. 414)
Below the arcuate line the transversus aponeurosis passes in front of rectus

Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses, including transversus, pass in front of rectus, leaving only transversalis fascia behind it.
Above the line, internal oblique splits around rectus. (Last's p. 414)
Transversus arises from the lateral two-thirds of the inguinal ligament

Transversus arises from the lateral half (one-third in some texts) of the inguinal ligament, not two-thirds.
Internal oblique takes the lateral two-thirds. (Last's p. 414)
The conjoint tendon attaches to the anterior superior iliac spine

The conjoint tendon attaches to the pubic crest and pectineal line, not the anterior superior iliac spine.
It reinforces the medial part of the posterior wall of the canal. (Last's p. 414)
Pyramidalis is supplied by T12

Pyramidalis and the lowest part of rectus abdominis are supplied by the subcostal nerve (T12).
Pyramidalis tenses the linea alba. (Last's p. 414)
The nerves run between internal oblique and transversus

The lower intercostal and subcostal nerves run forward in the neurovascular plane between internal oblique and transversus, as in the thorax.
Incisions that cut across them cause muscle weakness. (Last's p. 414)
T7 runs obliquely downwards in the sheath

T7 runs upward just below the costal margin, not obliquely downward in the sheath.
The lower nerves run progressively more obliquely downward. (Last's p. 414)
The ilioinguinal nerve enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring

The ilioinguinal nerve enters the inguinal canal from the side, by piercing internal oblique, not through the deep ring.
Then it emerges through the superficial ring. (Last's p. 414)
The genital branch of genitofemoral supplies cremaster

The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve passes through the deep ring into the cord coverings. It is motor to cremaster and sensory to the spermatic fasciae.
It forms the efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex. (Last's p. 414)
The ilioinguinal is sensory only within the canal

Within the canal the ilioinguinal nerve is sensory only; its motor fibres to internal oblique and transversus leave before it enters.
So injury in the canal causes only numbness. (Last's p. 414)
Damage to the ilioinguinal nerve in the canal weakens the conjoint tendon

Damage to the ilioinguinal nerve in the canal does not weaken the conjoint tendon, because its motor branch arises before the canal.
A Last's point. (Last's p. 414)
The testis has parasympathetic supply from the vagus

The testis has a sympathetic supply only (mainly T10), with no parasympathetic supply from the vagus.
The vagus does not reach the gonads. (Last's p. 414)

questions.s: Innervation of the peritoneum and gut (Last's):
o: Central diaphragmatic peritoneum is supplied by the phrenic nerve

The central diaphragmatic peritoneum is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5), so pain here is referred to the shoulder tip. The periphery is supplied by intercostal nerves.
Subphrenic abscess can cause shoulder pain. (Last's p. 414)
The obturator nerve is the chief supply of pelvic parietal peritoneum

The obturator nerve is the chief supply of the pelvic parietal peritoneum, so pelvic peritonitis may refer pain to the medial thigh.
Also seen with a pelvic appendix. (Last's p. 414)
Meissner's plexus lies between the muscle layers

The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus lies between the muscle layers; Meissner's plexus is submucosal.
Auerbach's controls motility, Meissner's secretion. (Last's p. 414)
Highly selective vagotomy cuts the nerves to the pylorus

Highly selective vagotomy cuts only the branches to the fundus and body; the nerves to the pylorus are preserved.
So emptying is maintained. (Last's p. 414)
The genitofemoral nerve emerges from its anterior surface

The genitofemoral nerve is the only branch of the lumbar plexus to emerge from the anterior surface of psoas. The obturator nerve and lumbosacral trunk emerge medially, the others laterally.
A useful identification rule. (Last's p. 414)
The obturator nerve emerges from its medial border

The obturator nerve emerges from the medial border of psoas, with the lumbosacral trunk.
It then runs along the pelvic side wall. (Last's p. 414)
The femoral nerve emerges from its medial border

The femoral nerve emerges from the lateral border of psoas, in the groove between psoas and iliacus.
The obturator is medial. (Last's p. 414)
It is supplied mainly by L4

Psoas major is supplied by L1 to L3, mainly L2, not L4.
L4 supplies more of quadriceps. (Last's p. 414)

questions.s: Quadratus lumborum and the lumbar fascia (Last's):
o: Quadratus lumborum lies in the anterior compartment of the lumbar fascia

The anterior and middle layers of the lumbar fascia enclose quadratus lumborum; erector spinae lies in the posterior compartment, between the middle and posterior layers.
Three layers, two compartments. (Last's p. 414)
The middle layer attaches to the tips of the lumbar transverse processes

The middle layer of the lumbar fascia attaches to the tips of the lumbar transverse processes; the anterior layer to their bases (front).
The posterior layer attaches to the spines. (Last's p. 414)
Psoas minor is present in about 90% of people

Last's says psoas minor is present in about two-thirds of people, not 90 percent.
It is absent in many. (Last's p. 414)
The psoas fascia is part of the lumbar fascia

Last's says the psoas fascia is not part of the lumbar fascia, though its lateral edge blends with the anterior layer.
A psoas abscess stays within its own sheath. (Last's p. 414)
It passes beneath the lateral arcuate ligament

The subcostal nerve and vessels leave the thorax behind the lateral arcuate ligament and run along the 12th rib in front of quadratus lumborum.
They then enter the abdominal wall. (Last's p. 360)
It lies behind the kidney

The subcostal bundle lies behind the kidney, with the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
These nerves can be irritated by renal disease, referring pain to the groin. (Last's p. 360)
The nerve lies above the vessels

The subcostal nerve lies below its vessels (vein, artery, nerve from above down).
The same order as in the intercostal spaces. (Last's p. 360)
The adrenal cortex arises from neural crest

The adrenal cortex arises from intermediate mesoderm; the medulla comes from neural crest.
Two different origins. (Last's p. 360)

questions.s: The fascia of the pelvic wall (Last's):
o: It covers obturator internus and piriformis

The parietal pelvic fascia covers obturator internus and piriformis and is firmly attached to the periosteum at their margins.
It forms the tendinous arch for levator ani. (Last's p. 360)
The sacral plexus lies behind it

The sacral plexus lies behind the parietal pelvic fascia, between it and piriformis.
Nerves lie outside the fascia. (Last's p. 360)
Pelvic nerves lie inside the fascia and vessels outside it

Last's principle is the reverse: nerves lie outside (external to) the fascia and vessels inside it.
So vessels must pierce the fascia to leave the pelvis. (Last's p. 360)
Sacral plexus branches to the buttock pierce the fascia

Because the sacral plexus lies behind the fascia, its branches to the buttock do not need to pierce it.
The gluteal vessels do pierce it. (Last's p. 360)
